title: Ghosts of Lessons Past Pt1
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien looks back at two lessons from his early career, a Community-based psychology lesson and a Simpsons-based law lesson, that took hours to prepare and produced enthusiasm but little learning. He uses the confessional format to argue that engagement is not learning, and that his postgraduate training had pushed him toward chasing engagement and learning-styles ideas. The lessons failed because students lacked the base knowledge needed to make sense of the video and answer the worksheet. He draws four lessons: much of his training was debunked, knowledge must be taught rather than caught, engagement does not equal learning, and flawed resources can sometimes be repaired by delivering content first and then checking understanding. He closes by tying the extraneous-load problem to ed-tech, citing The Digital Delusion. The piece works as a humane, first-person case for explicit instruction.
points: Engaging lessons can feel like success while producing no learning, because students buzzing about a lesson is not evidence that they understood it.
Prior knowledge has to be explicitly taught before students are asked to watch, interpret, and apply, so video-and-worksheet lessons fail when no base knowledge exists.
Learning tends to produce engagement through success feedback loops, which reverses the common assumption that engagement must come first.
When coaching experienced staff, the sunk cost of resource-building is large, so a flawed resource can be salvaged by sequencing content first and checking for understanding after each segment.
Novel media adds extraneous load and pulls attention from the content to be learned.
quotes: Secondly, knowledge must be taught, not caught. Students need to be explicitly taught the content before they can possibly answer a question about it. I was expecting students to watch a video and magically be able to understand it and then apply it to a completely different context.

Thirdly, engagement does not equal learning. I spent far too many years early in my career chasing the dragon of an engaging lesson and then wondering why my students were loving the class but their performance was poor.

Firstly, I know that almost anything I learned in my post graduate studies has been debunked (learning styles, multiple intelligences, left brain/right brain etc). Here was me trying to appeal to visual learners when I was never satisfying the need for a base knowledge to apply.

Finally, despite the fact I would never run a lesson similar to the above these days, the core idea could actually work with some tweaking. This is so important when pursuing change with experienced staff. The sunk cost of the time and effort teachers put into their resources is enormous.

Finally, the day comes and I run the lesson. Students aren’t laughing as much as I was hoping but they seem enthralled by the opportunity to watch a TV show in class for the purpose of learning. The episode ends, the students receive their worksheet but they’re slow to start.
Again, just like with Community, we watched the video, I handed out the worksheet, pens were slow to hit the paper. It wasn’t until years later I understood what I was doing wrong.
